Before I started writing, I went through every single infohazard skip on the site because they were my absolute favourites at the time. I remember this one stuck out to me because I was really disturbed by it. The idea of intestines being turned into food if I talked crap about a drawing just stuck to my mind and wouldn't get out. Something so simple being able to do this much damage to someone because of something so ordinary is what makes this so good to me.

Ramble over; +1 ad infinitum

item.title: Staff Post - Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

Yeah, yeah, I know "Eric" is a kind of Easter egg, but as we get more and more articles the chances of someone stumbling upon SCP-066, SCP-168, and SCP-683 in rapid succession to make the connection is getting kind of small. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

Once the .42 kilogram excision of tissue is complete, a brown "lunch" style paper bag (hereafter SCP-683-3) will appear in the interior of SCP-683-1. SCP-683-3 has consistently been labeled with the name "Eric".

To this:

Once the .42 kilogram excision of tissue is complete, a brown "lunch" style paper bag (hereafter SCP-683-3) will appear in the interior of SCP-683-1. SCP-683-3 has consistently been labeled with the name "Eric".

Changing this:

A 3" x 5" note card reading "Be a good boy today!" Ink is black and handwriting is consistent in style with the "Eric" written on SCP-683-3's exterior

To this:

A 3" x 5" note card reading "Be a good boy today!" Ink is black and handwriting is consistent in style with the "Eric" written on SCP-683-3's exterior

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.content:encoded:
"Exactly" like 002?

002 is 2000 cubic feet of sphere which converts anyone who enters it into furniture.

This is a refrigerator drawing which bites chunks out of people who make fun of it in order to prepare a chunk sandwich with the crusts cut off.

I'm really not seeing how this qualifies as even marginally related, let alone an "exact" match.

I would respectfully request that before you claim something is essentially identical to another entry, you explain your reasoning a little more. Otherwise your commentary might be interpreted as an accusation of plagiarism.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I didn't downvote for the picture, since it's definitely a personal preference. My main issue was the massive security problem posed by the artwork, but since you've addressed that, it's a neutral vote for me.

An article's suspension of belief is weakened when I see pictures that have captions explaining specific circumstances for why am anomaly looks a certain way. It makes it look like the picture was used for the sake of it, instead of providing a window of the author's personal perspective. Maybe the picture was cut off instead; the picture isn't indestructible, since fire can burn it, unless fire is the specific way to destroy this (what about chemicals, like acid?). And with image wizards like Faminepulse, maybe he could make it look realistic. So yeah, I guess that's why I found it "silly", since dozens of articles have superficial or oddly specific images.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This picture caption is kinda silly, given there is no evidence of anything that was burned on there.

Given that in the real world, these are two separate images, and I can't actually display the art on that particular refrigerator, I have to show pictures of the individual components. I thought it was valuable to explain why the image was not present on the refrigerator within the caption. Burning the image is referenced in the article, and is clearly pertinent to its anomalous effects. Did you want photoshopped char marks or something? That just doesn't seem necessary or realistic.

I don't really understand how this is "silly" or even an actionable critical comment, so it seems to be a personal preference of yours I can't really address. So…okay?

My main problem with this is the inclusion of SCP-683-2's picture in the article. Considering the infohazardous properties, why would they allow personnel to look at the picture and be able to make a judgement?

This is actionable, however. The parameters of viewing could be made clearer and the role of photographs outlined. I will look into that, as I hadn't really considered it before.

item.title: Who is Eric?
item.content:encoded:
SCP-006 "Eric's toy"

SCP-066 rolled away again and produced the phrase “Are you Eric?”

SCP-168

Upon initial inspection, it was discovered that the name “Eric” was carved into the inside of the removable casing.

Okay, I assumed this was a coincidence. Now I'm not so sure. What are the odds of three SCP items that bear or generate the name of the same kid? Shouldn't the Foundation try to figure out who this person was to ascertain a possible connection?
